questions.q: The chapter asks whether an entrepreneur's existing knowledge is enough to solve the problem at hand, or whether they need to seek other sources. Apply the chapter to answer.
questions.a: Sample: Existing knowledge is where an entrepreneur starts but rarely where the answer is found. The chapter defines an entrepreneur as someone who comes up with an idea and is resolute about solving a problem with an innovative solution -- and an innovative solution, by definition, is one that is not already known, so it cannot come entirely from what the person already has in mind. J.R.D. Tata shows this plainly: nothing in running a family business told him how to fly an airline, a thing nobody in India had done in 1932, so the knowledge had to be sought. The chapter's own account of the entrepreneur as the one who combines the factors of production points the same way, because combining them means hiring people whose expertise the entrepreneur does not personally hold -- the engineers and project managers it describes elsewhere. So the entrepreneur's own knowledge supplies the problem and the resolve; other sources supply much of the solution.
s: States that an innovative solution cannot come wholly from knowledge the entrepreneur already has
Uses evidence from the chapter, such as J.R.D. Tata starting an airline or the entrepreneur hiring expertise
Concludes with a balanced answer about what own knowledge supplies and what must be sought

questions.q: A startup is defined as a venture with limited resources aiming at rapid growth while leveraging technology. Apply this definition to explain why such a venture needs an entrepreneur more than a long-established business does.
questions.a: Sample: The definition itself contains the difficulty. Resources are limited, so every rupee and every hour has to be committed to one thing and not another, and there is no cushion if the choice is wrong -- that is exactly the risk-taking with money and time the chapter puts at the centre of entrepreneurship. Growth is meant to be rapid, so decisions cannot wait for certainty; somebody has to make key decisions regarding the operation and functioning of the business quickly and repeatedly. And leveraging technology means the venture is doing something in a way it has not been done before, so there is no established routine to follow and the problem has to be solved with an innovative solution. A long-established business has settled routines, a record, and enough resources to survive a mistake, so it can be run by managers following what already works. A startup has none of that, which is why the entrepreneur's judgement is the factor it depends on most.
s: Explains that limited resources make every decision risky, with no cushion for error
Explains that rapid growth forces repeated key decisions under uncertainty
Explains that leveraging technology means no settled routine exists, so innovation is required

questions.q: The chapter asks whether profit is the only motivation for an entrepreneur. Analyse the answer it gives, using J.R.D. Tata.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter's answer is no, and it builds the case in two steps. First it says directly that an entrepreneur derives a deep sense of satisfaction from seeing their dreams become a reality and from serving the people, which is a reward that no account book records. Then it gives a life that shows it: J.R.D. Tata believed businesses should not only make money but also help society, he was known for caring about his workers and providing good working conditions, and the honour he is remembered for is the Bharat Ratna in 1992, given for service to the nation rather than for profit earned. None of this denies that a business must earn -- the Tata Group grew into steel, cars, power and chemicals and had to be profitable to do so. The chapter's point is that profit is a condition of continuing, while the motivation can be the problem solved and the people served.
s: States the chapter's answer that profit is not the only motivation, citing the satisfaction it describes
Uses specific evidence from J.R.D. Tata's life, such as his belief about society or his care for workers
Distinguishes profit as a necessity for the business from motivation as the reason for doing it

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter places entrepreneurship alongside land, labour and capital rather than treating it as simply a kind of labour.
questions.a: Sample: Because what the entrepreneur does is different in kind from what a worker does. Labour is the physical and mental effort used in production, and a worker's effort is applied to a task that already exists and has been decided on by someone else. The entrepreneur's contribution comes before that: identifying the problem, choosing what will be produced at all, and gathering the other factors so that there is a task for anyone to do. Second, the entrepreneur bears the risk. A worker is paid for the effort whether or not the venture succeeds, while the entrepreneur invests money and time with no such assurance, and the chapter makes risk-taking one of the five defining tasks. Third, the entrepreneur makes the key decisions regarding the operation and functioning of the business, which is authority rather than effort. Effort, risk and decision are three separate things, and classing them together would hide the fact that production stalls if any one of them is absent.
s: Contrasts labour as effort applied to an existing task with the entrepreneur deciding what will be produced
Identifies risk-bearing as something the entrepreneur does and the wage-earning worker does not
Identifies decision-making authority over the operation of the business as a distinct contribution
Concludes that treating them as one would hide a distinct input production depends on

questions.q: The chapter asks whether entrepreneurship is the 'driving force' of production. Give your judgement, with reasons drawn from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: It is the driving force in the sense of what sets production moving, but not in the sense of being the most important factor. The case for it is strong: land, labour and capital exist in every town without producing anything until someone identifies a problem, combines them, takes the risk and decides how they will be used, and the chapter makes all four of these the entrepreneur's tasks. Nothing starts without that. But the chapter also insists that the factors complement each other and are interconnected, and that production becomes inefficient or halts if some are missing or misused. An entrepreneur with no capital raises nothing, with no skilled labour builds nothing, and with no land has nowhere to stand. So the honest verdict is that entrepreneurship is the factor that initiates and directs production while remaining as dependent on the others as they are on it.
s: Argues the case for entrepreneurship as the initiating factor, citing what the entrepreneur does
Sets against it the chapter's point that the factors are interconnected and that missing factors halt production
Reaches a clear, reasoned judgement rather than restating both sides

questions.q: Identify a real problem in your own neighbourhood and design an enterprise to solve it. Set out the problem, your innovative solution, the factors of production you would need, and the risk you would be taking.
questions.a: Sample: The problem -- schoolchildren in my colony have nowhere to leave their cycles safely, so many stop cycling and are driven instead, which adds to the traffic outside the school gate. The solution -- a small guarded cycle stand with a monthly pass, plus an on-the-spot puncture and brake repair service, so that leaving a cycle is both safe and useful. Land: a strip of unused ground beside the community hall, taken on rent from the residents' association. Capital: a metal frame and roofing, cycle stands, a lockable tool box and a starting stock of tubes and cables, funded by my savings and a loan from my uncle, with a bank loan only if that falls short. Labour: one trained attendant who can also do the repairs, whose skill is the human capital the business depends on. Entrepreneurship: my own -- I spotted the problem, and I will decide the monthly rate and the opening hours. The risk: I must pay the rent and the attendant every month whether or not enough families sign up, so if the stand is half empty in the first season I lose both the money and the time I put in.
s: States a real problem and an innovative solution to it
Identifies the land and capital the enterprise would need and where they come from
Identifies the labour required and the entrepreneur's own role
Names a genuine risk of money and time, as the chapter describes risk-taking

concepts.name: Technology as an enabler of production
concepts.description: Technology is the application of scientific knowledge. Every production activity uses some form of it, new technology often replaces old but not always, and platforms like SWAYAM and the National Career Service use it to remove geographical barriers to knowledge, skills and jobs.
concepts.idea: Technology is not a fifth ingredient poured into production -- it changes how much the other four can do.
concepts.rule: Technology means the application of scientific knowledge; a camera, for instance, converts light into electrical signals to create a digital image. Any production-related activity uses some form of technology, and some early forms that have existed since ancient times are still in use today. Newer developments make life easier: payments can be made at the click of a button through UPI, the Unified Payments Interface; farmers can get advance weather updates; and Global Positioning Systems can discover the shortest routes for transporting goods. Old technology often gets replaced by a new, better one -- email instead of letters by post, which is quicker and cheaper -- but technological progress does not always mean replacing old technologies, and some, like pulleys and wheelbarrows, are still in use. Technology also opens access to knowledge, skills and jobs: SWAYAM, which stands for Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds, is a Government platform offering courses for Grade 9 onwards free of cost and operating on MOOCs, Massive Open Online Courses, through which learners can explore subjects like robotics, aquaculture and textile printing at their own pace from anywhere, while the Government's National Career Service portal helps people find job opportunities across sectors from plumbing to accounting. In this way technology has eliminated geographical barriers.
concepts.example: Drones spray fertilisers to improve crop health and robots assist in surgical processes, while a wheelbarrow on a construction site and a pulley used in boats show that older technology has not been swept away.

questions.q: The chapter's Let's Explore asks you to think of technological advancements that have changed lives around you. Apply the chapter's framework to one such change, showing what it replaced and what it made possible.
questions.a: Sample: UPI has changed how money moves in my neighbourhood. It replaced cash carried in a pocket and the trip to a bank or an ATM to get it, and in shops it replaced the search for change, since the chapter notes that payments can now be made at the click of a button. What it made possible is larger than convenience: a vegetable vendor with no card machine and no counter can now be paid by anyone with a phone, so a very small enterprise can trade like a big one. It has also spread the reach of a business beyond the people who happen to be carrying notes that day. This is the chapter's point that newer technological developments are applied in various areas to make our lives easier, and its wider point that technology lets an enterprise do more without adding land, labour or capital.
s: Names a specific technological change and what it replaced
Describes what the change made possible that was not possible before
Connects it to the chapter's point about technology easing life or enabling more with the same inputs

questions.q: A district officer wants more young people in his district to find skilled work. Apply what the chapter says about SWAYAM and the National Career Service to design his plan, and state one thing technology alone will not solve.
questions.a: Sample: He should build the plan on the two platforms the chapter names. First, set up rooms with internet access in schools and panchayat buildings and enrol young people on SWAYAM, which offers free Government courses from Grade 9 onwards, running on MOOCs, in subjects like robotics, aquaculture and textile printing. Because the courses can be taken at one's own pace and from anywhere while pursuing other jobs, young people already working can join without giving up their earnings. Second, register the same group on the National Career Service portal, which lists jobs across sectors from plumbing to accounting, so that the skill they gain leads to work rather than a certificate. The chapter's claim that technology has eliminated geographical barriers is what makes both steps possible from a small district. What technology will not solve is the rest of human capital: a young person who cannot read well enough to follow a course, or who is too ill to attend, gains nothing from a free platform, so the officer still needs literacy classes and a working health centre behind the plan.
s: Uses SWAYAM correctly, including that it is free, online and self-paced
Uses the National Career Service to connect the skill gained to actual job opportunities

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter takes care to say that technological progress does not always mean replacing old technologies.
questions.a: Sample: Because the previous paragraph could easily be read as saying the opposite. It has just described old technology being replaced by a new, better one, with email displacing the posted letter because it is quicker and cheaper, and a reader could conclude that everything old is on its way out. The chapter blocks that by naming pulleys and wheelbarrows, which are ancient and still in daily use, and by saying earlier that some early forms of technology existing since ancient times remain in use today. The correction matters for the chapter's argument: if progress simply swept the old away, then India's ancient skill heritage and the techniques it describes would be worthless relics, and a producer would be foolish to keep any established method. Instead the test is whether a technology still does its job well for the inputs it consumes, and on that test a wheelbarrow survives while a posted letter does not.
s: Notes that the preceding example of email replacing post could suggest that new always displaces old
Cites the chapter's counter-examples, such as pulleys and wheelbarrows still in use

questions.q: The chapter presents technology both as something that makes production more efficient and as something that opens access to knowledge and jobs. Analyse how these two roles are connected.
questions.a: Sample: They are two ends of the same chain. In the first role technology works on production directly: it enables enterprises to produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs, as GPS does by finding the shortest routes and UPI does by settling payments instantly. In the second it works on people: SWAYAM puts free courses within reach of anyone with a connection, and the National Career Service puts job openings within reach of anyone looking, so that technology has eliminated geographical barriers. The connection is human capital. More efficient production needs workers who can run the newer methods, and the chapter has already said that human capital -- specialised skill, knowledge and expertise -- is what makes labour productive. The platforms are how that human capital is built at scale, and the efficiency is what it is built for. Take away the second role and the first stalls for want of people who can use the technology; take away the first and the training leads to jobs that do not exist. Each role supplies what the other requires.
s: Describes the first role, technology raising output from the same or fewer inputs, with an example
Describes the second role, technology opening access to knowledge and jobs, with an example
Identifies human capital as the link between the two roles
Explains that each role depends on the other, so neither works alone

questions.q: The chapter asks whether technology can replace other factors like labour, and whether that is good or bad. Give your judgement with an example.
questions.a: Sample: Technology can replace some labour but not the factor itself, and whether that is good depends on what happens to the people. The chapter's own example is agriculture, where increased machine use can lower dependence on labour: a harvester does in a day what a field of workers did in a week, and the same chapter says elsewhere that technology lets enterprises produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs. That is a real gain -- cheaper food and less back-breaking work. But the chapter also insists that human effort is involved at every stage of production, to design, supervise and improve, so the machine does not remove the need for people; it changes the kind of people needed, from many unskilled hands to fewer skilled ones. The change is good if those displaced can gain the new skills, which is exactly what the chapter's facilitators of human capital and platforms like SWAYAM exist to do, and harmful if they cannot, because then output rises while livelihoods disappear.
s: Gives an example of technology substituting for labour, such as machines in agriculture
Notes the chapter's point that human effort remains necessary at every stage, so the need shifts rather than vanishes
Reaches a judgement that makes the benefit conditional on retraining or access to new skills

questions.q: The chapter invites you to think of an invention that would solve a problem. Describe yours -- its name, what it does, how it works, and which factor of production it would help most.
questions.a: Sample: Name -- the Cool Crate. What it does: it keeps a vegetable vendor's unsold produce fresh overnight without a refrigerator, so that far less is thrown away. How it works: it is a double-walled clay crate with a gap between the walls filled with sand kept damp from a small tank on top; as the water evaporates through the outer clay it draws heat out of the inner chamber, so the inside stays several degrees cooler than the air. A small solar panel runs a fan that speeds the evaporation on hot days. It applies scientific knowledge -- the cooling effect of evaporation -- to a production problem, which is the chapter's own definition of technology. Which factor it helps most: land, in the chapter's sense of natural resources, because the vegetables come from soil and water and every crate thrown away wastes both. It also helps the vendor's capital, since less of her stock is lost. And like the pulley and the wheelbarrow, it is a simple technology that need not be replaced by a costlier one to do its job well.
s: Names the invention and states the problem it solves
Explains how it works in a way that applies scientific knowledge
Identifies which factor of production it helps and why
Connects the invention to a point the chapter makes about technology

concepts.name: How the factors of production are connected
concepts.description: The proportion of each factor used depends on the product, making work labour-intensive or capital-intensive. The factors complement each other, new techniques change the proportions, and supply chains link inputs across geographies -- and can break.
concepts.idea: The factors are not a list to be ticked off but a set of pieces that only work in the right proportions and only when the links between them hold.
concepts.rule: Land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and technology are combined to produce goods and services, and the proportion of each factor used depends on the product. Output from the agriculture, construction and handicraft sectors relies more on labour and is therefore labour-intensive, while semiconductor chips or satellites require more capital and specialised machinery and are capital-intensive. These factors complement each other and are interconnected; if some are missing or misused, production can become inefficient or be halted. New techniques can change the proportion used and the output: increased machine use in agriculture can lower dependence on labour, and 3-D printing can help revive dying art forms in textiles by producing handloom products on a large scale. The production inputs are available at different geographic locations, and enterprises can procure them from these varied locations and combine them, so geographic interconnectedness gives businesses access to varied inputs. The supply chain is a network of individuals, organisations, resources, activities and technology involved in the production and sale of goods, and a disruption in it, caused by relying on sources from far-off places instead of local inputs, results in a halt in the production process, as was the case during the COVID-19 pandemic.
concepts.example: The chapter's flow chart for mobile phone assembly runs from the R and D team conceptualising new features, through acquiring land and setting up a factory, acquiring raw materials, assembling components and installing software, testing the phone for functionality, quality and performance, to mass production and packaging and distribution to retail stores. India was the world's second-largest mobile phone manufacturer after China in 2025.

questions.q: During the COVID-19 pandemic many factories stopped work although they still had their buildings, machines and workers. Apply the chapter's account of supply chains to explain why.
questions.a: Sample: A factory is not a self-contained thing. The chapter defines a supply chain as a network of individuals, organisations, resources, activities and technology involved in the production and sale of goods, and every factory sits inside one. Because production inputs are available at different geographic locations, businesses procure them from far away, which normally gives them access to varied inputs but leaves them dependent on links they do not control. When the pandemic disrupted those links, the raw materials and components simply stopped arriving. The buildings, machines and workers were all still there, but the factors of production complement each other and are interconnected, so with one input missing the rest could do nothing and production halted. The chapter's own lesson is that relying on sources from far-off places, instead of local inputs, is what makes a disruption of this kind so damaging.
s: Defines or uses the supply chain as the network through which inputs reach a factory
Explains that inputs come from different geographic locations, so distant links can break
Concludes that with one factor missing the others cannot work, so production halts

questions.q: A state wants to attract satellite component manufacturing rather than more handicraft units. Apply the chapter's distinction between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production to advise it on what it must provide.
questions.a: Sample: The two need different things because the proportion of each factor used depends on the product. Handicraft units are labour-intensive: their output relies mainly on labour, so what they need most is people with craft skills, and a state can attract them with training, workshops and premises without heavy investment. Satellite components are at the other end -- the chapter names satellites and semiconductor chips as requiring more capital and specialised machinery. So the state must provide what capital-intensive production consumes: reliable power and land for large plants, the financial environment in which very large sums can be raised, and above all people who can run specialised machinery, which means engineers and technicians rather than numbers of workers. It must also secure the supply chain, since specialised components come from far-off places and the chapter warns that dependence on distant sources halts production when the links break. Attracting the second kind of industry is therefore a much larger commitment than attracting the first, and the state should be clear which it is choosing.
s: States that handicrafts are labour-intensive and identifies what such units need, chiefly skilled labour
States that satellite components are capital-intensive, needing capital and specialised machinery
Identifies what the state must provide for capital-intensive production, such as power, land, finance or technical skills

questions.q: The chapter says increased machine use in agriculture can lower dependence on labour. Analyse what this change does to the other factors of production on a farm.
questions.a: Sample: The change does not simply remove workers; it shifts the whole mix, because the proportion of each factor used depends on the product and the technique. Capital rises sharply, since a machine has to be bought or hired and then fuelled and repaired, so a farm that needed little capital now needs a great deal. Labour falls in quantity but rises in quality: fewer hands are needed, but someone must be able to operate and maintain the machine, which is human capital rather than simple effort. Land can be worked more intensively and in larger holdings, because a machine makes a bigger field manageable. And the entrepreneur's decisions become weightier, since the money is now committed in advance to equipment rather than paid out as it is earned. The chapter's point is that new techniques change the proportion used and the output, and this is what such a change looks like across all the factors at once.
s: States that capital requirements rise because machinery must be bought, fuelled and maintained
States that labour falls in number but needs more skill to run and maintain the machines
Notes an effect on land use or on the entrepreneur's decisions and risk

questions.q: The chapter says the factors work 'like puzzle pieces'. Analyse how well that image describes what it has told you about how the factors combine.
questions.a: Sample: The image captures two things well. It shows that the factors are different from one another and are not interchangeable, since a puzzle piece cannot stand in for another, and that the picture appears only when all of them are in place -- which matches the chapter's statement that if some factors are missing or misused, production becomes inefficient or halts. But the image is incomplete in an important way. Puzzle pieces come in fixed shapes and there is exactly one arrangement, whereas the chapter insists that the proportion of each factor used depends on the product, so agriculture and handicrafts are labour-intensive while semiconductor chips and satellites are capital-intensive. It also says that new techniques can change the proportion used, as machines do in agriculture and 3-D printing does in textiles. A puzzle cannot be reshaped in that way. The better reading is that the factors are like puzzle pieces in their interdependence but unlike them in being adjustable, and it is the adjustability that lets the same five factors build a farm and a satellite.
s: Explains what the image captures, such as the factors being distinct and all being needed
Links this to the chapter's point that missing or misused factors halt production
Identifies what the image misses, that the proportions vary with the product
Notes that new techniques can change the proportions, which a fixed puzzle piece cannot represent

questions.q: 'Businesses should buy their inputs locally rather than from far-off places.' Evaluate this using what the chapter says about supply chains and geographic interconnectedness.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter gives support to both sides, so the claim is half right. Against it, the chapter presents geographic interconnectedness as an advantage: production inputs are available at different geographic locations, and procuring from varied locations gives businesses access to inputs their own region simply does not have. A mobile phone factory cannot buy every component locally, and insisting that it should would make the product impossible. For it, the chapter warns that a disruption in the supply chain occurs due to relying on sources from far-off places instead of local inputs, and results in a halt in production, as happened during COVID-19. The sensible judgement is therefore not a rule either way but a balance: buy locally what can be bought locally, so that a break in a distant link does not stop everything, while keeping the distant sources that supply what no local producer can. The risk to be managed is dependence on a single far-off source, not distance itself.
s: Gives the case against the claim, that geographic interconnectedness supplies inputs a region lacks
Gives the case for it, citing supply chain disruption and the COVID-19 example
Reaches a balanced judgement rather than simply endorsing or rejecting the claim

questions.q: Draw up, in words, a flow chart like the chapter's for a product of your choice. Give the stages in order and mark at each stage which factor of production is chiefly being used.
questions.a: Sample: Product -- a wooden school desk. Stage 1, the owner decides on a design that is strong, stackable and cheap to repair: entrepreneurship, with the R and D thinking the chapter puts at the start of its own chart. Stage 2, rent a workshop with space for timber and a yard: land. Stage 3, buy the saw, planer, drill and clamps: capital. Stage 4, buy seasoned timber, screws and varnish: raw materials drawn from land, paid for with capital. Stage 5, two carpenters cut, plane and join the parts: labour, and their years of practice are human capital. Stage 6, check every desk for wobble, splinters and finish, as the chapter's chart tests the phone for functionality, quality and performance: labour, guided by the owner's standards. Stage 7, make a batch of fifty and stack them: labour and capital together. Stage 8, deliver to schools by hired truck: capital and the supply chain that links workshop to customer. Human effort runs through every stage, and the owner's decisions run over all of them, exactly as the chapter describes for the mobile phone.
s: Chooses a product and gives its stages in a sensible order, from conception to distribution
Marks each stage with the factor of production chiefly used
Includes a testing or quality stage and a distribution stage, as the chapter's chart does
Notes that human effort runs through every stage and that the entrepreneur guides the whole

concepts.name: Responsibilities towards the factors of production
concepts.description: Producers owe responsibilities to the natural resources they use and to the people they employ: sustainable use of limited resources, fair pay and safe conditions, training, workplace rights, and Corporate Social Responsibility.
concepts.idea: Using a factor of production is not the same as being free to use it up.
concepts.rule: When we produce goods we use natural resources like land, water and minerals, but these resources are limited and can be degraded if we are not careful. It is therefore important for producers to use natural resources responsibly, so that we can meet our needs today without making it harder for future generations to meet theirs; they should try to reduce waste, avoid pollution and protect the environment while making products, adopting sustainable practices that replenish natural resources for future use. Businesses also have responsibilities towards their workers and employees. Fair compensation and working conditions means ensuring that workers are paid fairly for their labour and work in a safe environment. Skill development and training means investing in training and education so that workers develop the skills necessary to remain competitive in the labour market. Workplace rights and protections means adhering to laws and regulations on workers' rights relating to fair treatment, preventing discrimination, and providing benefits like health care or paid leave. Businesses are also motivated to address social and environmental concerns through Corporate Social Responsibility, which includes reducing polluting activities, addressing the well-being of local communities, and treating employees and customers with respect.
concepts.example: In Tamil Nadu many people earn money working in leather factories, which helps the local economy, but the waste from these factories can pollute rivers and soil. When old smartphones are not recycled properly, harmful substances like lead and mercury can leak into the ground and water. India was the first nation in the world to bring a Corporate Social Responsibility law, in 2014, mandating companies to spend 2 per cent of their average profits of the last three years on CSR activities.

questions.q: An electronics company starts a scheme to collect and recycle customers' old phones. Using the chapter, explain three reasons why this is a responsible act.
questions.a: First, it prevents the harm the chapter names directly: when old smartphones are not recycled properly, harmful substances like lead and mercury can leak into the ground and water, and this pollution is dangerous for people, animals and plants. Second, it reduces waste and protects the environment, which the chapter says producers should try to do while making products. Third, recycled materials can be used again as inputs, which is a sustainable practice that helps replenish natural resources for future use instead of drawing fresh minerals from limited stocks. It also counts as Corporate Social Responsibility, since it reduces polluting activity and benefits the local community.
s: Names the specific harm avoided, such as lead and mercury leaking into ground and water

questions.q: The chapter's Think About It asks how local communities and biodiversity are affected by polluting production. Apply the chapter to answer, using one of its own examples.
questions.a: Sample: Take the leather factories of Tamil Nadu. The local community gains first, because many people earn their living there and the local economy is helped, so the factories are not simply a bad thing for the people around them. But the waste from the factories can pollute rivers and soil, and that falls on the same community. Water they drink, wash in and irrigate with is affected, and soil that is degraded yields less, so farming households near the factory lose what the factory workers gain. Biodiversity suffers in the same way, since the plants and animals living in and along the river have nowhere else to go; the chapter makes the same point about lead and mercury from unrecycled phones being dangerous for people, animals and plants alike. The result is that the benefit and the harm land on overlapping groups, which is why the chapter treats responsible production as a duty rather than a choice.
s: Uses a chapter example and notes the benefit it brings, such as earnings and the local economy
Traces the harm to the local community through polluted water or degraded soil
Traces the harm to biodiversity, noting that plants and animals cannot move away

questions.q: Ratna's restaurant has grown and she now employs twenty people. Apply the chapter's three responsibilities towards workers to say what she should put in place.
questions.a: Sample: Under fair compensation and working conditions she should pay each of the twenty fairly for the work they actually do, and make the kitchen safe -- guarded equipment, ventilation over the stoves, and a floor that is not slippery -- because a restaurant kitchen is where most of the risk sits. Under skill development and training she should invest in training so her staff develop the skills necessary to remain competitive in the labour market: sending a cook to learn new dishes, teaching hygiene and food safety properly, and letting a helper train up to a cook's role. That serves her too, since the chapter says human capital is the quality and efficiency of labour. Under workplace rights and protections she should adhere to the laws on workers' rights -- treating everyone fairly, preventing discrimination in who is hired or promoted, and providing benefits such as health care or paid leave so that an illness does not cost a worker her livelihood. Together these are what the chapter says a business owes the people whose labour it uses.
s: Applies fair compensation and working conditions with concrete measures for a restaurant
Applies skill development and training, noting that workers must remain competitive in the labour market
Applies workplace rights and protections, including fair treatment, non-discrimination and benefits such as health care or paid leave

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter puts responsibilities towards workers in the same section as responsibilities towards natural resources.
questions.a: Sample: Because both are factors of production and the chapter is making a single point about all of them. Land and labour are two of the four inputs a business uses, and the section's title is responsibilities towards factors of production, not towards the environment. A producer who pollutes a river is running down an input that is limited and can be degraded; a producer who underpays workers, leaves the workplace unsafe or never trains anyone is running down an input too, because the chapter has already shown that human capital is built by training and health and lost when they are absent. In both cases the business takes the benefit now and leaves the cost to be paid later, by the next generation in the one case and by the workers and the wider labour market in the other. Putting them together makes the argument general: whatever a business uses to produce, it has a duty to keep in good condition rather than consume.
s: States that both natural resources and workers are factors of production the business uses
Shows that neglecting either runs down an input, degrading resources or failing to build human capital
Draws the common point, that the benefit is taken now while the cost falls later or on others

questions.q: India made CSR spending a legal requirement in 2014, yet the chapter also says businesses are 'motivated' to address social and environmental concerns. Analyse the relationship between the law and the motivation.
questions.a: Sample: The two are not the same thing and the chapter keeps both. The motivation is what the chapter describes when it says businesses address social and environmental concerns to benefit society and biodiversity, by reducing polluting activities, caring for the well-being of local communities and treating employees and customers with respect. That is a matter of what a company chooses, and the chapter's own example of J.R.D. Tata -- who believed business should help society and cared for his workers' conditions -- shows it existing long before any law. The law does something different: by mandating 2 per cent of average profits of the last three years, it sets a floor that applies to companies whose owners feel no such motivation at all, and it makes the amount predictable rather than dependent on goodwill. The risk is that a floor becomes a ceiling, with companies treating 2 per cent as the whole of their duty and their remaining conduct as their own affair. So the law guarantees a minimum and the motivation is what carries a company beyond it; India's distinction in being first, in 2014, lies in not leaving the matter to motivation alone.
s: Describes the motivation as voluntary, citing what CSR includes or an example such as J.R.D. Tata
Describes what the law adds, a binding minimum of 2 per cent of average profits of the last three years
Identifies a tension or risk, such as a minimum being treated as the whole duty
Reaches a conclusion about how law and motivation work together

questions.q: 'A factory that gives people jobs has already done its duty to the community.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The claim is not empty. The chapter says that entrepreneurs create job opportunities and support livelihoods, and its Tamil Nadu example acknowledges that many people earn money in the leather factories and that this helps the local economy. Employment is a genuine contribution. But the chapter does not let it stand as the whole duty. The same factories' waste can pollute rivers and soil, harming the very community that holds the jobs, and producers are told to reduce waste, avoid pollution and adopt sustainable practices so that future generations can still meet their needs. Nor is a job by itself enough for the worker: the chapter requires fair pay, safe conditions, training and workplace rights including benefits like health care or paid leave, so a badly paid job in a dangerous workshop does not discharge the duty either. The verdict is that giving jobs is the beginning of a business's responsibility and not the end of it, which is exactly why India's law of 2014 asked for something more.
s: Concedes the real value of employment, citing job creation and support for livelihoods
Argues what the claim leaves out, such as pollution, sustainability, fair pay, safety or workers' rights
Reaches a clear judgement that employment is a beginning rather than the whole duty

questions.q: Write a short responsibility charter for a small factory in your town. Include two commitments about natural resources and two about workers, and say for each how someone outside the factory could check that it was being kept.
questions.a: Sample: Charter for the Kamala Steel Utensils Works. Natural resources, commitment one: no untreated water leaves this factory. We will pass all wash water through a settling and treatment tank before it reaches the drain, as the chapter shows industrial wastewater being recycled before release. Anyone can check it by testing the water at our outflow pipe, which we will keep open to inspection. Commitment two: we will buy back and reuse scrap metal from our own products and from the town's households, so fewer fresh minerals are mined and less waste is dumped, which is the sustainable practice of using recycled products as inputs. This can be checked against our purchase register, which will show the weight of scrap bought each month. Workers, commitment one: every worker is paid at or above the agreed rate by the seventh of the month, and no machine runs without its guard fitted -- checkable from the wage register and by an unannounced walk through the shop floor. Commitment two: each worker gets twelve days of paid leave a year and one week of paid training, so that skills stay competitive in the labour market -- checkable from the leave and training records, which we will display each year.
s: Gives two commitments about natural resources drawn from the chapter, such as avoiding pollution or reusing materials
Gives two commitments about workers drawn from the chapter's three responsibilities
Gives a practical external check for each natural resource commitment
Gives a practical external check for each worker commitment
